description: Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Having become brahman, serene in self, one neither grieves nor desires and is the same toward all beings; one then attains supreme devotion (18.54).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Asked whether his delusion born of ignorance is destroyed (18.72), Arjuna reports: delusion destroyed, memory (smṛti) regained by Kṛṣṇa's grace, standing firm with doubt gone, ready to do his word (18.73).
The relinquisher (tyāgin), pervaded by sattva, intelligent, with doubts cut away, neither hates disagreeable action nor clings to agreeable action (18.10).

Sañjaya calls the dialogue wondrous and hair-raising (romaharṣaṇa) (18.74); recalling it again and again he rejoices again and again (18.76); recalling Hari's most wondrous form, great is his amazement (vismaya) and he rejoices again and again (18.77).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Sāttvic happiness is delighted in through practice, ends sorrow, is like poison at first and nectar in the end, and is born of the serenity of the understanding of the self; rājasic happiness, from sense-contact, is nectar at first and poison in the end; tāmasic happiness deludes the self first and last and arises from sleep, sloth and heedlessness (18.36–39).
